t.2.93.1: Once the army had encamped, Bharata, full of eagerness, then set out to see his brother, pointing out the way to Śatrughna as he went.
t.2.93.3: Sumantra, too, followed close behind Śatrughna, for he, like Bharata, was filled with a longing born of the wish to see Rāma.
t.2.93.2: Having instructed the sage Vasiṣṭha, “Bring my mothers quickly,” he, devoted to his elders, swiftly went on ahead.
t.2.93.4: Then, even as he was going along, the glorious Bharata saw his brother's leaf-hut, standing amid the dwellings of ascetics, and the hermitage cottage.
t.2.93.5: Then, in front of that hut, Bharata saw pieces of wood that had been broken off and flowers that had been gathered.
t.2.93.7: Then, even as he was going, the mighty-armed and radiant Bharata, filled with joy, spoke to Śatrughna and to all those ministers.
t.2.93.8: I think we have reached that region of which Bharadvāja spoke, for I think the river Mandākinī is not very far from here.
t.2.93.6: And in that forest he saw great heaps made from the dung of deer and buffaloes, piled up as a remedy against the cold.
t.2.93.10: And here, on the flank of the mountain, is the ground trodden by mighty elephants with lofty tusks as they roared at one another.
t.2.93.9: These strips of bark have been tied up high by Lakṣmaṇa; this must be the path he marked with signs, wishing to go out at an untimely hour.
t.2.93.11: Yonder is seen the thick, billowing smoke of that black-trailed fire which ascetics in the forest constantly wish to kindle.
t.2.93.12: Here, filled with joy, I shall see my noble brother Rāghava, that tiger among men who pays due honour to his elders, as one would behold a great sage.
t.2.93.13: Then, after going toward Citrakūṭa for a short while, that Rāghava reached the Mandākinī and spoke these words to that company of people.
t.2.93.14: That tiger among men, the lord of the people, having come to a desolate place, sits upon the bare ground, intent on the hero's posture. Shame on my birth, together with my life!
t.2.93.15: Because of me, the lord of the world, Rāghava of great splendor, has met with misfortune; giving up all his desires, he dwells in the forest.
t.2.93.16: Thus reviled by the people, today I shall fall again and again at the feet of Rāma and of Sītā, seeking to win their favor.
t.2.93.17: Lamenting thus in that forest, the son of Daśaratha beheld a large, holy and charming hut made of leaves.
t.2.93.18: It was covered with many leaves of sāla, tāla and aśvakarṇa trees, spacious, and strewn with soft kuśa grass, like an altar at a sacrifice.
t.2.93.19: It was adorned with bows that resembled the weapon of Śakra, bows able to bear heavy strain, gold-backed, of great strength, and tormentors of enemies.
t.2.93.20: He saw the hut adorned with fearsome arrows lying in their quivers, gleaming like the rays of the sun, as Bhogavatī is adorned with serpents whose mouths blaze with fire.
t.2.93.21: It was resplendent with two swords and their two coverings of fine gold, and adorned as well with two shields variegated with drops of gold.
t.2.93.23: There in Rāma's dwelling Bharata saw a sacred altar, broad and with a blazing fire, sloping toward the north-east.
t.2.93.22: He saw the hut, hung with bright finger-guards of iguana hide adorned with gold, unassailable by hosts of enemies, as a lion's cave is to deer.
t.2.93.25: And he saw Rāma seated close by, wearing a black antelope skin and clad in garments of rags and bark, like a fire.
t.2.93.24: Having gazed about for a moment, Bharata saw his revered elder, Rāma, seated in the hut, wearing a crown of matted locks.
t.2.93.27: The mighty-armed one, seated like the eternal Brahmā on a sacrificial ground strewn with darbha grass, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.93.26: Him with shoulders like a lion's, mighty-armed, with eyes like white lotuses, the lord of the earth bounded by the ocean, who walks in the way of dharma.
t.2.93.28: Seeing him, the glorious Bharata, overwhelmed by grief and bewilderment, ran toward him, the righteous-souled Bharata, son of Kaikeyī.
t.2.93.29: And having seen him, he lamented in anguish, his voice choked with tears; unable to hold himself steady through fortitude, he spoke these words.
t.2.93.30: He who deserves to be waited upon by his subjects in the royal assembly, this elder brother of mine, now sits here attended by the wild beasts of the forest.
t.2.93.32: He who once wore many kinds of bright and varied flowers, how does this Rāghava now bear this burden of matted locks?
t.2.93.31: That great-souled one, who was formerly accustomed to garments worth many thousands, now wears here a pair of deerskins as he practises dharma.
t.2.93.33: He who could gather a store of merit through sacrifices performed as prescribed now seeks a dharma born of the body's hardship.
t.2.93.35: Because of me, Rāma, who is accustomed to happiness, has met with this sorrow. Shame on the life of cruel me, a life condemned by the world!
t.2.93.34: How is it that the body of the noble one, whose body was once anointed with costly sandalwood paste, is now covered with dirt?
t.2.93.36: Lamenting thus in his misery, his lotus-face drenched with sweat, Bharata, weeping, fell down before he could reach the feet of Rāma.
t.2.93.37: Tormented by grief, the mighty prince Bharata, having once piteously uttered "Noble one!", said nothing more.
t.2.93.38: With his throat choked by tears, he beheld the illustrious Rāma and cried out only, "Noble one!", and after that he could not speak.
t.2.93.39: Śatrughna too, weeping, saluted the feet of Rāma; and Rāma, embracing them both, also shed tears.
t.2.93.40: Then in the forest the two princes met with Sumantra and with Guha, just as the sun and the moon meet in the sky with Śukra and Bṛhaspati.
t.2.93.41: Seeing those princes, who resembled leaders of elephant herds, gathered together there in the great forest, all the forest-dwellers too abandoned their joy and shed tears.
